title: Exceptions, Error Values, and Failure Signals
learningObjectives: Describe the main idea and its role in reliable program behavior.
Recognize the topic in code or a real-world programming scenario.
Trace the relevant behavior and identify the likely outcome.
Explain a common mistake, risk, or limitation.
Apply the concept and verify the result with a suitable check.

understand.concept: Programs communicate failures through different mechanisms: exceptions, returned error values, status codes, rejected promises, result types, or language-specific signals. An exception may interrupt normal control flow unless it is caught. A failure value can be handled explicitly by the caller. These mechanisms are not interchangeable across languages.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing the failure signal helps determine where to handle it, what information to preserve, and whether execution can safely continue.
understand.analogy: A delivery process may report a failed delivery using a notice, a returned package, or a status in a tracking system. Each signal gives the next person information, but software failure signals have specific language and API rules.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a simplified comparison; software failures and recovery depend on language, runtime, system boundaries, and context.

explain.narrative: Identify what a function promises to return on success and how it signals failure. Follow the signal to its caller. Preserve meaningful context, distinguish expected failures from programming defects, and ensure callers do not mistake a failure for a valid result.

examples.title: Explicit status value
examples.code:
function divide(a,b){ if(b===0) return {ok:false,error:'zero divisor'}; return {ok:true,value:a/b}; }
console.log(divide(8,2).value);
examples.explanation: The caller receives a result object and can inspect its status.

examples.title: Inspect failure status
examples.explanation: A status flag distinguishes success from failure.

examples.title: Throw an exception
examples.code:
function requireName(name){ if(!name) throw new Error('Name required'); return name; }
try { console.log(requireName('Asha')); } catch(e) { console.log(e.message); }
examples.explanation: The exception interrupts the function and is caught by the caller.

examples.title: Promise rejection
examples.explanation: A rejected promise is handled through its rejection path.

examples.title: Preserve context
examples.code:
function load(){ throw new Error('Database unavailable'); }
try { load(); } catch(e) { console.log('Load failed: '+e.message); }
examples.explanation: A handler adds useful context without discarding the original reason.

commonMistakes: Catching exceptions but returning an indistinguishable success value.
Using exceptions for routine branching without considering the language design.
Assuming every API signals failure in the same way.
